options: A mathematical framework for representing, analysing and solving problems involving interconnected data
A technique for drawing bar charts
A method for compressing image files
A spreadsheet formula language
A style of database indexing used only in finance
questions.explanation: Graph theory is a mathematical framework widely applied to real-world problems involving interconnected data, studying vertices connected by edges.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT listed as a field where graph theory is applied?
options: Social networks, to analyse relationships and influence
Cooking, to combine recipe ingredients
Biology, to map genetic networks and protein interactions
Transportation, to improve route planning and traffic flow
Project management, to visualise tasks and dependencies
questions.explanation: The listed application fields are computer science, social networks, biology, transportation and project management; cooking is not among them.

questions.stem: In the three-city example of graph theory, where A is connected to B and B is connected to C, what is the degree of vertex B?
questions.explanation: B has two connections, one to A and one to C, so its degree is 2, while A and C each have a degree of 1.

questions.stem: Graph theory groups its tools under three headings. Which set is correct?
options: Tables, rows and columns
Input, process and output
Nodes, weights and colours
Properties, structures and relationships
Ingestion, transformation and serving
questions.explanation: Graph theory addresses the properties, structures and relationships between data elements.

questions.stem: What real-world analogy is used for a directed graph (digraph) in graph theory?
options: Cities on a map
Two-way roads
Bus stops
Distances in kilometres
One-way streets
questions.explanation: Directed graphs, where edges have a direction, are likened to one-way streets, whereas undirected graphs are likened to two-way roads.

questions.stem: In the three-city graph, what happens to connectivity if vertex B is removed?
options: A and C will no longer be connected
A and C become directly connected
The graph gains a cycle
The degree of A increases to 2
Nothing changes
questions.explanation: B is the only vertex linking A and C, so removing it means there is no longer a path between A and C and the graph is no longer connected.

questions.stem: In graph theory, what is a path?
options: The weight assigned to an edge
A sequence that shows how to move from one vertex to another
A vertex with the highest degree
The removal of a vertex from a graph
A pair of vertices that are not connected
questions.explanation: A path is a sequence showing how to move from one vertex to another, for example A to B to C.

questions.stem: If an edge from C back to A is added to the graph A to B to C, what is formed?
options: A bipartite graph
A disconnected graph
A cycle: A to B to C to A
A tree
A weighted graph
questions.explanation: Adding an edge from C to A produces a path that starts and ends at the same vertex, which is a cycle.

questions.stem: When is a graph described as connected?
options: When every edge carries a weight
When it has at least one cycle
When all edges have a direction
When there is a path between every pair of vertices
When it has exactly three vertices
questions.explanation: A graph is connected if there is a path between every pair of vertices, so all vertices can be reached from any other vertex.

questions.stem: In the school bus analogy for graph theory, with Stop 1 to Stop 2 being 2 km and Stop 2 to Stop 3 being 3 km, what do the vertices, edges and weights represent, and how long is the path from Stop 1 to Stop 3?
options: Vertices are roads, edges are stops, weights are times; the path is 6 km
Vertices are pupils, edges are timetables, weights are fares; the path is 2 km
Vertices are buses, edges are drivers, weights are speeds; the path is 3 km
Vertices are stops, edges are roads, weights are distances; the path is 1 km
Vertices are bus stops, edges are roads between stops, weights are distances; the path is 5 km
questions.explanation: In the analogy, vertices are bus stops, edges are roads and weights are distances, so the path from Stop 1 to Stop 3 is 2 km + 3 km = 5 km.
